claims.statement: Deep Agents follows a trust-the-LLM model, so containment belongs in installed tool implementations, backends, or sandboxes; HITL is opt-in, StateBackend does not execute shell commands, and LocalShellBackend is an explicit higher-power opt-in.

FilesystemPermission rules validate absolute patterns, resolve read/write access by ordered first match with allow as the default, enforce deny before backend execution, filter denied bulk-read entries, and apply conservative subtree-overlap denial for potentially recursive deletion.

Filesystem interrupt permissions are converted separately into HumanInTheLoopMiddleware routing: exact tools use first-match interrupt resolution, bulk tools conservatively interrupt on intersecting subtrees and bypass-prone omitted, current-directory, absolute-glob, or parent-traversing patterns, and approved or edited calls still re-enter tool-level denial enforcement.

dcode stores a per-thread approval mode fail-closed to Manual, routes side-effecting tools through its HITL predicate, and uses AutoModeHITLMiddleware to combine deterministic policy, classifier review, denial errors, and escalation to human review.

dcode's ask_user tool pauses from tool execution, validates resumed answers before attaching an authorization receipt, and requires exception-catching middleware to preserve GraphBubbleUp so the graph interrupt is not swallowed.

Talon's ToolApprovalStore persists a validated exact-name boolean policy in a bounded regular non-symlink JSON file; enabled entries yield approve/reject interrupt configuration, updates are locked revision compare-and-swap operations, and invocation snapshots isolate an in-flight graph from saved changes.

Talon validates that every interrupt in a batch has a unique resumable ID before prompting, cancels valid MCP elicitation separately after unique-key validation, aggregates all ordinary action requests into one handler decision, and fans that outcome out into one explicit resume payload; malformed batches and a 50-round limit fail rather than implicitly resuming.

Talon derives the operator context required to change approval policy from trusted channel exposure rather than request metadata, requires active invocation context as well, keeps approval and external authorization callbacks separate, and accepts channel approval replies only from the initiating sender while reactions also require matching provider, conversation, prompt message, and sender.

Scheduled invocations and background-result deliveries do not retain an interactive approval or OAuth path: the host marks delivery as unattended and withholds both handlers, while the runtime independently clears operator context for cron or delivery and auto-rejects protected calls in those contexts, including when an approval handler is injected.

Detached background subagents clear operator and authorization context and report an interrupted protected action as not run; cron-only inline delegation instead executes within its already unattended caller, disallows nested delegation, and cannot inherit an interactive approval or authorization handler.
TalonHost stores one pending approval future by agent conversation, prompts through the channel, removes the pending entry when it resolves, and only completes it from an accepted reply or reaction.

dcode's asynchronous HITL middleware reads the thread-scoped approval mode after model completion and uses a private in-process routing marker so checkpointed graph state cannot forge an autonomous approval decision; YOLO bypasses gated interruptions while Auto only bypasses them in eligible graphs.

Talon creates its default approval policy only when the policy file is missing, and that default enables send_message alongside policy, conversation, MCP-server, and async-task management tools; an existing valid policy is retained unchanged.

The ACP demo exposes session modes whose selected mode builds the agent's interrupt map: ask_before_edits gates edits, writes, todos, and execute; accept_edits gates todos and execute; and accept_everything supplies no interrupts.

Talon is an experimental alpha runtime rather than a production or enterprise security boundary; it lacks complete production-grade HITL approval policy, channel administrator controls, and multi-tenant isolation, and its opt-in sandbox does not cover MCP tools.
